chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:

The man may recite the Azan while he is seated, but he may not recite the Iqamah except while he is standing; and you may recite the Azan while you are riding, but you may not recite the Iqamah except while you are upon the ground.

key_terms.يُؤَذِّنُ: He recites the Azan (call to prayer)
key_terms.يُقِمْ: He recites the Iqamah (call to establish prayer)

ai.seo_question: Can the Azan be recited while sitting or riding, and does the Iqamah require standing?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Rida (AS) delineates the distinct legal statuses of the Azan and Iqamah, emphasizing that while the Azan is a proclamation adaptable to one's state (seated or riding), the Iqamah is an act of immediate establishment requiring the reciter to be standing on the ground. This distinction highlights the Iqamah's role as the direct precursor to the physical act of prayer, thereby requiring a posture of readiness and stability, whereas the Azan serves as a broader announcement. The ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that the Iqamah is intrinsically linked to the commencement of the prayer itself, necessitating a more formal physical presence than the Azan.
